trap.wrong: "Write every location update to the main database and query it for nearby drivers."
trap.why: That's over a hundred thousand writes per second of data that's stale within seconds, crushing a transactional database built for durable, consistent writes.
trap.probe: Separating hot current state from history, in-memory geospatial indexes, streaming ingestion and smoothing noisy GPS.
trap.say: "Current location goes to a sharded in-memory geospatial index with short TTLs for matching; the full stream goes through Kafka to cheap storage for history and analytics; and noisy GPS is filtered and snapped to roads before use."

thesis: Location updates are high-volume, short-lived data. Keep only the latest position per driver in an in-memory, sharded geospatial index for real-time queries, stream all updates to durable cheap storage for history, and clean noisy GPS before it drives decisions.
pitch: Each driver app sends its position every few seconds over a persistent connection or lightweight HTTP. An ingestion tier validates and authenticates updates and publishes them to a stream partitioned by driver or region. A location service consumes the stream and maintains each driver's latest position, status and timestamp in an in-memory geospatial index, sharded by region, with entries expiring if a driver stops reporting. Matching and 'drivers near me' queries hit that index. The same stream lands in object storage or a time-series store for trip reconstruction, analytics, disputes and ETA model training, at far lower cost than a transactional database. GPS is noisy, especially in dense cities, so I'd filter outliers, smooth with a Kalman filter or similar, and map-match to roads. Riders watching a car approach get updates pushed through a subscription channel for that trip, not by polling. Clients adapt update frequency, more often when on a trip, less when idle, to save battery and bandwidth.

points.d: Latest position in memory for real-time queries; full history in a stream and cheap storage.
Updates published to a partitioned stream decouple ingestion from consumers (matching, ETA, analytics).
Region-sharded cells with TTLs so offline drivers disappear automatically.
Outlier filtering, smoothing and map-matching to roads before using positions for ETAs and billing.
Riders tracking a trip subscribe to that driver's position channel instead of polling.
More frequent updates during trips, less when idle, balancing accuracy with battery and cost.
Trip-critical events (pickup, drop-off) recorded transactionally; raw pings are best-effort.

decision: In-memory geospatial index for the latest position, a partitioned stream for fan-out, and object or time-series storage for history; never the transactional database for raw pings.
numbers: 500,000 drivers updating every 4 seconds ≈ 125,000 updates/s; at ~100 bytes each that's ~12.5 MB/s, ~1 TB/day of raw history before compression.
pitfalls: Raw pings into the main database.
No TTL, so offline drivers appear available.
Using unfiltered GPS for fares and ETAs.
Riders polling for driver location every second.

followups.q: How do you compute the fare distance if GPS is noisy?
followups.a: Use map-matched trip paths from the cleaned history, with fallbacks to routing estimates where data is missing.

followups.q: What happens when a region's location shard fails?
followups.a: Replicas or rapid rebuild from the stream (latest positions arrive within seconds anyway), with matching degraded briefly in that region.

followups.q: How do you handle drivers in tunnels or with poor connectivity?
followups.a: Dead reckoning from last speed and heading for a short time, and marking positions as estimated.

example: A ride-hailing startup wrote every GPS ping to Postgres; at 40,000 drivers the database saturated. Moving latest positions to Redis GEO sharded by city with 30-second TTLs, and streaming raw pings to Kafka and S3, removed the database load and made history cheap to keep.
